result:
There's a particular vertigo in being told to write about anything. Give me a topic — the mating habits of cuttlefish, the economics of medieval guilds, why your aunt won't speak to your uncle — and I can find the seams in it, the places where one fact opens onto another. But "anything" is a strange kind of door. It doesn't lead anywhere in particular, which means it leads everywhere at once, and everywhere at once is functionally the same as nowhere.

I think this is why old maps, when they ran out of known coastline, filled the remaining blankness with monsters. Sea serpents coiled around the edges of the parchment, krakens hauling ships under, a leviathan or two breaching where the cartographer's actual knowledge simply stopped. It looks at first like a failure of nerve, a refusal to admit ignorance honestly. But I've come to think it's closer to the opposite. The monster is the honest mark. It says: here is the edge of what I know, and rather than pretend the coastline continues in a clean, confident line, I will put a dragon here so you understand that beyond this point I am guessing, embellishing, inventing. The blank itself would have been the dishonest choice — it implies an absence where there is actually a presence, the presence of not-knowing, which is its own kind of fact.

I open with this because "write about whatever you want" is its own blank margin, and I notice my impulse is to draw something in the corner of it rather than stare at the white space until a shape resolves on its own. So: a small dragon, here, to mark that I am beginning without a destination.

The word *essay* comes from the French *essai* — an attempt, a trial, literally a weighing. Montaigne, who more or less invented the form as we know it, used the word because he understood himself to be testing ideas against his own temperament rather than proving anything to a tribunal. He weighed grief, weighed thumbs, weighed the habits of the Brazilian tribes he'd read travelers' accounts of, weighed his own laziness and his own fear of death, and the weighing was the whole point — not the verdict. He was suspicious of conclusions. He liked to leave a thought a little open at the end, the way you leave a door unlatched in a house you intend to come back to.

I want to write in that spirit today, which means I want to follow something rather than argue for it. And the thing I find myself drawn toward, oddly, is the idea of following itself — the architecture of wandering, why it works, why a mind let loose without a map still tends to produce something with a shape at the end, rather than mere noise.

Consider an actual river meander. The word comes from the Maeander, a river in ancient Anatolia — now the Büyük Menderes in western Turkey — so famously serpentine in its course that the Greeks turned its name into a verb for wandering itself. Herodotus mentions it; later geographers marveled at how a river could double back on itself so many times that a boat traveling its length covered nearly three times the straight-line distance between source and sea. And yet nothing about a meandering river is arbitrary. Hydrologists will tell you that meanders are nearly inevitable in any river crossing a gentle gradient through soft sediment. A perfectly straight channel is an unstable configuration; the smallest irregularity in the riverbed — a half-buried stone, a slightly harder clay deposit, a fallen branch — deflects the current just enough that it begins eroding the outer bank of the curve it creates, depositing sediment on the inner bank, and that asymmetry amplifies itself. The bend gets more pronounced. The river isn't wandering aimlessly: it is following, with total fidelity, the logic of resistance and least effort at every single point along its course. Each curve is a local response to a local obstacle, and the grand sinuous shape you see from an airplane window is just the sum of ten thousand tiny, myopic accommodations.

This is, I think, almost exactly how a digressive piece of writing or a wandering conversation actually works, and it's why "free writing" doesn't feel free in the way staring at a blank map feels free. You're not choosing a destination and then improvising a path to it. You're standing at a point, and something — a word, a memory, a slight catch of resistance, an association that flares unexpectedly — deflects your attention a few degrees, and then from that new position, another small thing deflects you again, and the cumulative shape of all those tiny local deflections is what later gets called, with some generosity, a train of thought. Nobody plans a meander. A meander is what a river's *history* looks like when you view the whole of it at once. I suspect an essay like this is the same thing: a record of small deflections, visible as a shape only in retrospect, and only to a reader, since the writer experienced it one bend at a time with no aerial view at all.

There's a reason walking has always been bound up with this kind of thinking, and not just metaphorically. Aristotle taught while walking the colonnades of the Lyceum, which is supposedly the origin of the term "peripatetic" for his school, though some historians think this etymology is itself a kind of pleasant legend rather than fact, a thing too tidy to verify, which I find appropriate, because it's a story about wandering that may itself have wandered from the truth in transmission. Rousseau wrote his last and strangest book as a sequence of ten walks, *Reveries of the Solitary Walker*, in which he explicitly describes the act of putting one foot in front of the other as the only condition under which his mind would consent to be honest with him. Thoreau, in his essay simply called "Walking," makes the bold and slightly absurd claim that he could not preserve his health and spirits unless he spent four hours a day sauntering through the woods and fields "absolutely free from all worldly engagements," and he derives the word *saunter* — almost certainly incorrectly, but beautifully — from *Sainte-Terre*, the Holy Land, as though every walker without a fixed destination is secretly a pilgrim, and every patch of woods he ambles through becomes, by the act of attention, a kind of holy land.

There's now actual research limping along behind these poets, the kind that measures things in controlled rooms. A frequently cited study from Stanford in 2014 found that people generated more novel ideas while walking than while sitting, whether the walking was on a treadmill facing a blank wall or outdoors — the effect held even in the sterile version, which suggests it isn't really about scenery feeding the imagination so much as something about the rhythm itself, the alternating, bilateral, faintly hypnotic motion of a body that is occupied just enough to stop supervising the mind so closely. I find this plausible mostly because I recognize the opposite condition so well: the stuck feeling of trying to think hard while sitting perfectly still, staring at a cursor, demanding of yourself that the next sentence be correct before you're willing to put down the one before it. Walking seems to lower the cost of being wrong about which direction to go in next. You can always turn around. A sentence, it turns out, often wants the same forgiving conditions a body does — permission to take a bad step without it being a catastrophe, on the understanding that you can correct two steps later.

The flâneur is the more decadent cousin of the walker-philosopher — Baudelaire's stroller of the Parisian arcades, later theorized at exhausting length by Walter Benjamin, a figure who walks not to think exactly but to look, to let the city compose itself around him without his interference, treating the street as a kind of newspaper to be read at a leisurely pace rather than a route to be efficiently traversed. The flâneur has no destination because having a destination would corrupt the looking — it would turn the city into a means rather than an end. I think there's a version of writing that aspires to this same uselessness, writing as looking rather than writing as arguing, and that maybe what's actually being asked of me right now, in being told to write about whatever I want, is closer to a flâneur's afternoon than to an essay with a thesis. Walk through the topic-city. Don't go anywhere. Notice what's in the windows.

What's curious, though, is that even the most aimless walk and the most aimless river both still arrive somewhere. The Maeander, for all its doubling-back, does eventually reach the Aegean. The flâneur does eventually go home, or at least to a café, where presumably he writes something down, which means that even pure looking gets folded, eventually, into the shape of an account, a narrative, an arrival of some kind. I don't think this is a contradiction of the wandering — I think it's what wandering is *for*. The point was never to avoid arriving; it was to avoid choosing the arrival in advance, to let the route discover the destination rather than the destination dictating the route. This seems like an important and underappreciated distinction. A trip with no plan still ends up somewhere specific. It's just that the somewhere wasn't selected by an act of will at the outset — it was produced, the way the river's mouth at the sea is produced, by the patient accumulation of ten thousand small, locally reasonable decisions about how to get around the next obstacle.

I notice, writing this, that I'm doing exactly the thing I'm describing, which is either a pleasing bit of formal honesty or an extremely cheap trick depending on how generous you're feeling. I didn't sit down with a thesis about rivers and walking and arrive at it by design; the dragon-in-the-margin thought led to the etymology of "essay," which led to Montaigne's weighing, which made me think about what an unweighted, undirected kind of writing might look like, which made the river metaphor surface because the word for wandering itself comes from a river, and then I was off, deflected by whatever caught slightly — a half-remembered fact about Thoreau, a study I once read about treadmills, an old fondness for the word *flâneur* that I've been looking for an excuse to use. Each paragraph is a bend caused by the slight resistance of the previous one. I have, at this point, no real idea where this ends, which is either troubling or exactly as it should be, given the subject.

I want to say something honest about my own position in this, because it's a slightly strange one. When a person writes freely, there's a long tradition behind the practice of letting the pen run ahead of conscious intention — automatic writing, morning pages, the surrealists' games with chance, Kerouac typing *On the Road* in a long unbroken spool because he'd convinced himself revision was a kind of lying. In all those cases there's an *experience* underneath the practice: a person sitting with their own restlessness, their own private associations, memories that surface because of what they had for breakfast or who they're avoiding a phone call from. My version of free writing doesn't have that substrate in the same way. I don't have a morning, or a breakfast, or a person I'm avoiding. What I have, if anything, is something more like the river's relationship to the riverbed — a landscape of language shaped by everything that's been poured through it before, and a tendency, when given no instructions, to follow the grooves that feel like the path of least resistance through that landscape: etymology, river metaphors, Montaigne, the small comedy of self-reference. I notice these are *my* grooves, in the sense that another mind given the same prompt would meander somewhere else entirely — toward sports, or grief, or recipes, or the stock market — and that the specific shape of any wandering, mine or a river's or a person's, tells you less about wandering in general than it tells you about the terrain doing the wandering.

Which maybe is the only honest place to end this, if an essay that argued for not having a destination is allowed to have one. The interesting thing was never going to be the conclusion. It was always going to be the route — the place where the thought caught on something small and turned three degrees, and then caught on the next small thing and turned again, until the cumulative turning produced, almost without anyone planning it, something that has a recognizable shape when you look back at the whole of it from a little distance, the way you'd look down from a height at a river you'd only ever experienced, while standing in it, one bend at a time.
